text: Which chord pattern is the standard 12 bar blues?
correct: I I I I | IV IV I I | V IV I I
wrong: I IV V I | I IV V I | I IV V I
I I IV IV | V V I I | I IV V V
ii V I I | ii V I I | IV V I I
explanation: The 12 bar blues is built on chords I, IV and V: four bars of I, two of IV, two of I, then V, IV and two bars of I. Other simple I, IV, V progressions are also common.
tip: 12 bar blues = I I I I | IV IV I I | V IV I I.

text: What is "call and response" in the blues?
correct: A vocal phrase answered by the lead instrument, such as guitar or harmonica
wrong: Two singers performing the same melody a third apart
A drum fill that signals a change of section
A repeated bass riff under a sustained chord
explanation: Call and response is a conversation between the voice (the call) and a lead instrument such as guitar or harmonica (the response).
tip: Call and response: voice asks, instrument answers.

text: Which description best fits early Country Blues recordings such as those of Robert Johnson?
correct: Mono, scratchy and noisy, with poor separation because the musician was recorded with one source
wrong: Stereo recordings with a separate microphone on every instrument
Clean multitrack recordings overdubbed in a purpose-built studio
Digital recordings with heavy artificial reverb
explanation: Early blues was captured on mono discs with lots of surface noise. Musicians were gathered around a single recorder or microphone, so instruments are not separated.
tip: Early blues = mono, scratchy, surface noise, poor separation.

text: What changed in the mid 1920s that improved the sound of blues records?
correct: Electrical recording with microphones replaced purely acoustic horn recording
wrong: Multitrack tape recording replaced mono discs
Digital sampling was introduced
Stereo vinyl LPs became the standard format
explanation: Before 1925 performers played into an acoustic horn. Electrical recording using microphones captured a wider frequency range, and quality improved again after 1945.
tip: c.1925: acoustic horn → electrical microphone recording.

text: Why was the metal-bodied resonator guitar popular with early blues players?
correct: Its metal resonator cone made the acoustic guitar much louder before electric amplification
wrong: It could be plugged straight into a valve amplifier
It produced a clean, quiet tone ideal for studio vocals
It had two necks so it could play bass and lead
explanation: The resonator cone amplifies the string vibrations acoustically, so the guitar cuts through in noisy venues and on early single-microphone recordings.
tip: Resonator = louder acoustic guitar via a metal cone.

text: What does slide (bottleneck) guitar technique produce?
correct: A continuous, voice-like glide between pitches
wrong: Rapid hammered-on notes with no sustain
Muted percussive chords only
Notes that are always exactly in tune with the frets
explanation: A glass or metal slide is moved along the strings, creating smooth glissandi that imitate the human voice. It is especially associated with Country Blues.
tip: Slide guitar = vocal-like glissando; typical of Country Blues.

text: Why did Chicago Blues musicians such as Muddy Waters adopt electric guitar and amplification?
correct: To be heard in noisy urban clubs and to give the guitar and harmonica lead-instrument power
wrong: Because acoustic guitars were banned in Chicago
Because record labels required all blues to be played on piano
Because amplification removed the need for a drummer
explanation: Chicago Blues introduced electric guitar, bass guitar, drums and amplified harmonica. Amplification let the band be heard over crowds and gave the instruments a strong lead voice.
tip: Chicago Blues = electric guitar, bass, drums, amplified harmonica.

text: How did Little Walter create his famous overdriven harmonica sound?
correct: He played through a hand-held microphone into a small guitar amp pushed into overdrive
wrong: He recorded onto wax cylinders and sped them up
He used a Hammond organ and Leslie speaker
He added a digital delay pedal after recording
explanation: Cupping a microphone and driving a small valve amp into overdrive gave the harmonica a thick, distorted, saxophone-like tone.
tip: Amplified harp = mic + small valve amp driven into overdrive.

text: What produces the natural overdrive on Chicago blues guitar recordings?
correct: Small valve amplifiers turned up until the valves clip and the speaker compresses the signal
wrong: A built-in digital distortion chip
Tape speed being changed during mixing
A plate reverb unit set to maximum
explanation: The worksheet notes little use of effects apart from distortion. That distortion came from pushing valve amps beyond their clean headroom, adding warm harmonics and compression.
tip: Distortion = pushed valve amp, not a pedal.

text: Which Chicago label, run by Leonard and Phil Chess, recorded Muddy Waters and Howlin' Wolf?
wrong: Sun Records
Motown
Atlantic Records
explanation: Chess Records of Chicago released the key electric blues artists, with Willie Dixon as bassist, songwriter and talent scout.
tip: Chess Records = Muddy Waters, Howlin' Wolf, Willie Dixon.

text: What does the career of the Rolling Stones show about the history of the blues?
correct: The blues was passed back and forth across the Atlantic between black and white musicians
wrong: The blues was invented in Britain and exported to America
The blues stopped being played in America after 1960
The blues has never influenced rock music
explanation: The blues began as a mix of European, American and African styles and was exchanged across the Atlantic by artists including B.B. King, the Rolling Stones, Chuck Berry, Jimi Hendrix, Eric Clapton and Led Zeppelin.
tip: Cultural exchange: blues ↔ British blues ↔ rock.

text: How did Moby's album Play show the influence of blues field recordings?
correct: It sampled old blues and gospel field recordings from the Lomax archive and combined them with electronic beats
wrong: It was recorded live on wax cylinders
It used no samples and only live blues musicians
It was a straight cover of Chicago blues songs
explanation: Moby sampled historic recordings, turning the noise and character of early mono field recordings into part of a modern production. The worksheet highlights sampling (Moby) as a modern blues influence.
tip: Modern link: sampling old blues recordings (Moby).
